episode.episode: Philips Hue: The smart home’s light bulb moment
episode.showDescription: Version History is a show about the best gadgets ever. And the worst ones. And the ones that might have changed the world, if they ever actually shipped. Every week, your favorite people from The Verge and beyond hang out to tell and debate the story of a gadget, app, website, or any other tech product, and try to determine the item’s true legacy. Because not every product is a hit, but every product has a story. And the ones that really matter aren’t always the ones you think. From the Verge and the Vox Media Podcast Network.
episode.episodeDescription: The humble light bulb might be the ultimate success story in the smart home. Our connected, adaptable homes are supposed to be customizable, connected to everything, and incredibly easy to use, and nothing has made that work quite like Philips Hue lights. In this episode, The Verge's David Pierce and Jennifer Pattison Tuohy are joined by smart home journalist and expert Richard Gunther to tell the Hue's story. We trace the product's history from its origins in the smartphone revolution, try to figure out how Philips managed to turn a staggeringly expensive lightbulb into a must-have gadget, and look at whether there's even more invention left in the future of lighting. We’re also on video! Check us out on YouTube. Subscribe to The Verge for unlimited access to theverge.com, subscriber-exclusive newsletters, and our ad-free podcast feed. We love hearing from you! Email your questions and thoughts to vergecast@theverge.com or call us at 866-VERGE11. Learn more about your ad choices. Visit podcastchoices.com/adchoices

transcript_window.text: And bring your space.
Look at TV.
A Philips Living Colors Iris is the perfect way to...
just gives you the sense of the time we're talking about.
High -power LEDs deliver 16 million colors to choose from.
And with the easy -to -use remote control, you can adjust brightness to set the mode you want.
It's timeless and distinctive.
So this gives you a sense, right?
This is very much a smart lamp, but it is a sort of hacky pre -smartphone digital one.
But you can change the color of your light.
And this is already a meaningful, exciting new thing.

And so there's a team at Philips that is like, OK, wouldn't it be cool if you could change the colors on your light with this touchscreen that people are starting to have in their pockets called the iPhone?
And then there's this other team working on the living color stuff led by this guy named George Yanni, who, Jen, you just spoke to the other day.
In fact, George, who is the co -founder of Hue, is a theoretical physicist.
physicist.
So, and he was brought on in order to help understand like complex systems, which is what they were starting very early days to design.
The team had started coming up with new interfaces, new ways to interface with your lights because they saw this potential.
Now that we had a digital light experience or the potential of a digital light experience, so many more ways of interacting instead of just flipping a switch.
I actually was using the iPhone to prototype new remote control interfaces because I could then update them very quickly rather than have to get new tools made every time I wanted to do a user test.

But in playing around with these interfaces on the phone, all web interfaces back then, there was no App Store, we found actually this is a great way to control our lights because we can make it customizable, right?
the lamps we're controlling.
We can have people, you know, choose their favorite colors, store scenes.

And so we kind of quickly pivoted towards a pitch, which became an internal startup within Philips for actually having smartphones and digital interfaces be a new way of interacting with lights inside our home.
And that was kind of the core idea, like, how can we develop more ways or better interfaces for lighting.
And as they were trying to develop this, they spun out this team to be just focused on this, what was essentially a software project.
And then as they started to develop it, they realized this was a really core idea.
